hook_say: Everyone blames takeout. In this example September, takeout went just $14 over its budget, while the five biggest checkouts made up almost half of everyday spending.

rows.label: Everyday spending, September
rows.say: Here's one month of everyday spending: $1,231.
rows.why: Groceries, eating out, gas, household, fun and the rest, not rent or bills.
rows.tts: Here's one month of everyday spending. About twelve hundred and thirty bucks.

rows.label: Takeout, 5 orders
rows.tts: Five takeout orders. Two hundred fourteen dollars.
rows.ask_tts: [short pause] So... takeout broke the budget?

rows.label: Takeout over its $200 budget
rows.say: Nope. It was budgeted at $200, so it went over by $14. Fourteen.
rows.tts: Nope. It was budgeted at two hundred dollars, so it went over by fourteen bucks. Fourteen.

rows.label: 4 grocery trips + 1 clothes order
rows.say: Now the five biggest checkouts: four grocery runs and one clothes order. $581.
rows.why: Four grocery trips ($141.07, $132.18, $118.64, $109.53) and one clothes order ($79.99).
rows.tts: Now look at the five biggest checkouts. Four grocery runs and one clothes order. Five hundred eighty-one dollars.

rows.label: Share of everyday spending
rows.say: That's 47% of everyday spending. In five swipes.
rows.why: The tracker lists the five biggest everyday spends each month, so you see where the money really went.
rows.tts: That's forty-seven percent of everyday spending. [short pause] In five swipes.
